pages.title: Gangue
pages.text: Rock is not metal. What a lump of ore yields comes with the stony part that was never metal, and that part becomes slag sitting in your bath.$p$pRich ore is the cleanest at roughly 5-8% of the bath, normal 8-13%, poor 10-17%, and the small fragments you sweep off the ground 12-20%.

pages.title: You Cannot See It
pages.text: Nothing on the item tells you how dirty this particular lump is, and two lumps of the same grade differ a little from each other. The only honest reading is the Slag line in the crucible after they are in there.$p$pMelting refined metal instead brings its own history: flawed scrap keeps the slag it was cast with.

pages.title: So What
pages.text: Smelting straight from rock always gives Flawed metal, because the slag is over the 2% line before you have done anything wrong with the ratio.$p$pThere are two ways out of that. Lift the slag back out of the bath with a bowl and a flux, or take the dirt out of the rock before it ever goes near a fire.$p$pWashing is the cheaper habit once you have a barrel, and the only way to fill a crucible from a heap of poor ore without drowning it.

pages.title: The Quern Grounds It, the Water Cleans It
pages.text: TFC's quern already breaks a lump into **ore powder**: seven scoops from a rich lump, five from a normal, three from a poor, two from the small fragments, and every scoop is worth five mB of metal.$p$pGround on its own buys nothing. Melt the powder and it gives up the same five mB with all of the stone still in it - about **12% of the bath** - and it has lost the one thing that made it worth picking, its grade: nothing on a scoop says which vein it came from.$p$pSo a scoop of ground ore is only ever worth smelting when you have no barrel to wash it in.

pages.title: Washing Is the Paying Step
pages.text: Five scoops of powder and a drink of water in a barrel come out as one **concentrate**, worth the whole twenty-five mB they carried between them: the wash spends no metal at all, it only spends the quern stroke and the water.$p$pAnd it takes the dirt with it. A concentrate brings **no slag into the bath whatsoever**, so a crucible filled from washed copper and washed tin pours clean bronze, clean brass, clean silver - with no skimming, no flux and no second pass.$p$pThat is the reward for building the barrel and the grinding stone. Everything the flaw system can still reach you, it reaches through the metal you already melted: re-smelted scrap keeps its defects, and a pot never pours cleaner than ten percent.

pages.title: Only the Heavy Minerals Wash
pages.text: Water sorts by weight, so it takes the ores whose mineral is far heavier than quartz: hematite, limonite and magnetite, cassiterite, malachite, and native copper, gold and silver.$p$pSphalerite, bismuthinite, tetrahedrite and garnierite are not much heavier than the rock they sit in. Their powder can be smelted, and it cannot be cleaned - those you have to skim in the bath, or flux, the way everybody did before a barrel was worth building.
